utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: May it please the Court. After he does, may I be heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stein?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, we are prepared to proceed with Mr. Ellis, but I should note for the record that we got his provisional summary at 8.35 this morning and his final proofing summary five minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we have heard this before. It is in addition to what you have already received. It is a helpful document because it focuses minds on all sides as to what the witness should be saying. Clearly, there is a problem about getting it around if the witness, as usual, has only come in the night before, but I'm sure the Prosecution have heard what's ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Full name, rank, and present position, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: I am Major John Richard Ellis. I am the staff officer grade two responsible for information management at headquarters, Kosovo IV, currently based in Pristina, Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Deployed with the Cheshire Regiment at the end of 1992 to Bosnia, did you become the liaison officer for Kakanj, Visoko, Olovo, Breza, and Vares shortly after Christmas 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've laid on the ELMO the map that I know some of the Court are using as a general map for reference, if the focus can be as large as possible. To set your task in a geographical context, can you, in summary but identifying towns and roads as you go along, explain in a couple of sentences your area of operation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: My area of responsibility was almost exactly from the junction, what was called the Zenica junction, with the road to Vitez going to the west and Kakanj to the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, pausing there, at the moment, the focus of the map isn't very clear. What we can see is Zenica at the top, just point to it --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: (Indicating)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- and then Kakanj to the east. Thank you. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: From there, my responsibility extended west -- wrong, east and south covering the town of Kakanj, from Kakanj, again east again up through Haljinici to Kraljevska Sutjeska, just off the map, and south down to Visoko, and from Visoko further across to Breza and Vares. Vares is almost due east from Haljinici and Kraljevska Sutjeska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The nature of your duties was what?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: I was the liaison officer with the responsibility for trying to maintain an open route for aid convoys and military traffic to move from Vitez, Stara Bila, through to the Tuzla salient.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To do that, did you make and keep contact with local military and/or political personalities?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Yes, with a number of them. It was essential to the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of your work, did you get to know the HVO commanders of both Vares and Zepce?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was their attitude towards Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: The commander in Vares was exceptionally anti, the reasoning being that he had an ongoing feud with the Muslim RBiH commanders to the south from Visoko and from Breza, to the extent that he accused them a number of times of committing attempts on his life in the form of a car bomb and close quarter assassination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Zepce?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Zepce was a political appointee who made significant efforts to point out that he was very anti-Muslim and would do what he could to make life difficult for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want you to deal in a moment with what you knew of the attitude of Dario Kordic in Busovaca, but before I come to that, it will be necessary for you to tell us one or two things about the deployment of certain brigades. In order to do that, can we substitute for the general map a black and white copy of the portion of it that you're looking at, which will become Z2612.8? If you, Major Ellis, can have a red marker, I think it will probably show up on the black and white map. Can you tell us, please, about the disposition of certain brigades? First, the Jajce Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: The Jajce Brigade had originally been moved following the fighting in Gornji Vakuf as part of a settlement to the area of Biljesevo, which is located --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you mark it and put "J" for Jajce in a big mark?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: -- located in a school to the south of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The ArBiH 319 Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: The 319 Mountain Brigade was the permanent resident brigade in Kakanj, and its headquarters was located in the centre of Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you just write "319," again for ease of reference?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then the 3rd Battalion of the 7th Muslimanski Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: The 3rd Battalion of the 7th Muslimanski Brigade originally were based in the Sretena Hotel but subsequently moved to a school about one kilometre west of the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you mark that as "3/7" for our convenience?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your judgement, did the disposition of these brigades have some effect on the attitude of Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I object. Objection unless there is a proper foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question is perfectly proper. The witness can answer, giving the basis of his knowledge for his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first question then, please, is one that you can answer "Yes" or "No."

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course. In your judgement, did the disposition of these brigades have some effect on the attitude of Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: In my opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want you now, please, to give us your sources of knowledge for Dario Kordic's attitude.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: The primary source of my knowledge was a Lieutenant Neven Maric, who was the commander of the Kotromanic Brigade, which was based to the east of Kakanj at the village of Haljinici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you mark that, please, on the map, and it would be as well, I think, to mark him by reference to his brigade which could be "KO," I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us more about him.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Neven Maric had been a computer specialist in the JNA. He had very good working relationships with the commander of 319 Brigade in Kakanj. They had served together. In fact, the commander of 319 Brigade, a Major Hadzic Dzemal, had been his instructor at a JNA officer school. Neven Maric was under orders that should it be required, he was to conduct a relief operation towards Busovaca by mounting an offensive operation from Haljinici west through the lines of control and crossing the road south to Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pausing there, and I don't think it will be necessary for you to mark the map, but with the pointer can you show, for clarity, what his orders would have involved his doing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: He would have been required to mount an offensive operation from the area of Haljinici and the hills to the north and south (indicating), west through the area of Kakanj, which was moderately built up and urbanised, and carrying on up the high ground to link up with the Croat forces that were in the area here in positions along this high ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In what circumstances, as you understood it, would these orders have come into effect so that he would have been obliged to carry out that manoeuvre?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: The orders would have come from his superior headquarters at Vares. The trigger for those orders I was not privy to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, did you give that young officer some advice or an opinion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Yes, I did give my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Namely?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: That to do such an attack would be exceptionally foolhardy, to lead a under-strength brigade through an urban area against certainly two battalions of veteran battle-hardened troops. Particularly the Jajce Brigade were very tough fighters indeed, and the 3rd Battalion of the 7th Muslimanski Brigade were noted for being shock troops and they were known as the Muslimanski Brigade because they had a reputation of being religious zealots, and to take an under-strength brigade into that terrain against those sort of forces would have been tantamount to suicide.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In any event, was he ever obliged to carry out this manoeuvre?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Not during my time in Bosnia, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's one of your sources of information upon which you formed your view. Was there another?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: There was. His name was Captain Matthew Dundas-Whatley. He was the liaison officer for the area of Travnik, Turbe, along the Lasva Valley to Zenica, and inclusive of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What, if anything, was he able to tell you about the effect of the disposition of these Muslim troops on Busovaca and Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: The significant fact was that the movement of the Jajce Brigade upset the balance of power in the area. Up until then, there had been a status quo. The arrival of the Jajce Brigade and 3rd Battalion of the 7th Muslimanski Brigade made Dario Kordic quite nervous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just pause there, please. Can we find out when it was that the Jajce Brigade arrived? Can you help, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you able to help the Court with that question; when, to your knowledge, did the Jajce Brigade arrived at the position you've indicated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. In detail, I cannot remember precisely, Your Honour. I can remember the incident very clearly, in that I turned up at the headquarters prior to the section commander Ganic Nehru arriving, to his surprise with a bottle of whiskey, which I then shared with the incoming commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You can't give the date precisely. Can you, at this stage, put some parameters on the date and point us to documentation that may be able to give the date more precisely?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It was at least ten days to two weeks prior to the incident at Ahmici, which would place it before the 1st of April. It was subsequent to the settlement of the fighting in the area of Gornji Vakuf, which I believe took place in early February, late January, early February, just as the roads were becoming passable, I believe subsequent to the death of Lance Corporal Wayne Edwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Documentation that will help us pinpoint it with greater precision would include what?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Record of the aid delivery of the NGO Feed The Children, who made a delivery of approximately two tons of baby food for the families of and children who had arrived at the village of Biljesevo, the milinfosums of the 1 Cheshire battle group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And include a reference to the arrival of the Jajce Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Yes. There was an operation mounted to escort the Jajce Brigade from the area of Gornji Vakuf into the area of Biljesevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. We'll find that, and that should answer that question. You've mentioned the killings at Ahmici. One matter of detail. Did you, on the days before those killings, drive along the Kakanj-to-Vitez road?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Yes, on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you drive at a regular and, as it were, predictable time or at random?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Fairly regular times, the reason being you went out after breakfast, you had to get to a number of meetings, or I had to get to a number of meetings, which meant a fairly early start. Battalion policy at the time meant that I had to recover, by about 5.00, 5.30 in the evening, in order to take part in the battalion conference and update so that everyone was aware of the various activities that were going on within our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of your journeys along that road in the days leading up to the events at Ahmici, did you observe either troop movements or any other out-of-the-ordinary events?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the night of the 15th/16th of April itself, where were you staying?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: I was sharing a house just to the east of the main encampment within Stara Bila, approximately 100 metres south-southeast from the school building itself at Stara Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you ever meet Kordic in person?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there one incident that you can tell us about where his name came to be mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Yes. After --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll come to that in a minute.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In an attempt to date that incident, what parameters for dates would you put on it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: I cannot remember the date of the incident exactly. However, it was at least five to six days after Ahmici, so around about the 20th of April. I don't believe it was more than three weeks later than that, so probably the 10th of May. There is documentary evidence which will tie it down significantly more tightly than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you only came in last night, and we have yet to tie down and find the documents concerned?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They are being searched at the moment. The incident occurred whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: The precise location was from the turn-off -- the Busovaca turn-off, which is located here (indicating) on the map, roughly two or three kilometres to the west, somewhere along that stretch of road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This has to do with a convoy, so would you please mark that again for our assistance with, I think, "C" for "Convoy"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: (Witness complies)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you first became involved, what was the state of play?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: I was driving east at about 4.00 in the afternoon, having had a meeting with Lieutenant Neven Maric in Kakanj. I came upon a single truck that was parked across a road. To the northern side of the truck was a steep cliff. To the southern side was a roadside cafe with a parking area, but the access to it was blocked. There was a fairly sheer drop to the southern side, so the road was fairly well balanced on both sides. As I approached, I noticed three, I believe, vehicles containing journalists. Certainly one Land Rover. I can't remember the other two vehicles. I got out and spoke to them, and they said the road was blocked. I moved down into the roadside cafe, adopting a deliberately low-threat approach, not putting on my body armour, not putting on my helmet, not taking my rifle, to appear non-threatening, and I took my interpreter with me. We met the local commander who was an HVO commander, whose name I don't know, and I noticed on the far side of this truck a convoy of UNHCR vehicles or, wrong, civilian trucks which were being used by the UNHCR, and they were escorted by two Warrior armoured infantry fighting vehicles, one at the front and one at the rear. Around the trucks was a group of HVO soldiers, probably about 10 to 15 initially, although that number increased later. The truck itself that was blocking the road, I was informed by the HVO commander, had been booby-trapped, and I could see chains were being used to disable it and immobilise that vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the convoy had been stopped by what process, as you could judge it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Basically, it was impossible to drive through. The truck was blocking the road. The truck was allegedly booby-trapped. Without --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How had the truck got between the convoy and the guarding vehicles of the Cheshires?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No, the truck was not between the infantry fighting vehicles, it was in front of. The convoy was made up of a Warrior at the rear, a number of trucks, ten or so, although I don't recall exactly, and a Warrior at the front. In front of the whole package, there was a vehicle across the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was in charge of the Warrior or Warriors?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: In the lead Warrior, there was a young Cheshire platoon commander whose name I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were the two Warriors in a position to communicate one with another and to solve this problem?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: When I arrived, the two Warriors were not in sight of each other, although they had radio communications. Neither of the Warriors had anybody who could speak Serbo Croat, so there was no interpreter capability with that convoy. The young commander had basically buttoned up, i.e., closed down the vehicle, and was waiting for something to happen. I believe he had reported back, but I'm not in a position to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What further steps did you take?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Because I had an interpreter with me, I immediately started talking to the commander, trying to find out what was happening, why he had stopped the convoy. My concern was two-fold; first of all, to get the convoy through and, secondly, to get the journalists out of the way and through on their way. I asked permission to do the first, and that was agreed, and I was able to get the journalists from the eastern side of the roadblock across to the western side, where they then waited. My negotiations to free the convoy met with significantly less success. I tried to make it very clear to the local commander, who appeared quite junior, that as far as I was concerned, all U.N. vehicles had been given right-of-way along this road, and that had been agreed by both Mate Boban and Dario Kordic. When I made that point, he was quite surprised. He said his orders had been from Dario Kordic to stop that convoy. I then remonstrated with him and said, "I'm a liaison officer. I can go and speak to your superior commanders and we can get them released," and he wasn't budging. He didn't really care who I spoke to. I then got on the radio back to our headquarters and asked for deployment of our quick reaction force, a force of four Warrior fighting vehicles with a platoon of infantry. I also asked for the appropriate liaison officer who I know worked with Dario Kordic, Matthew Dundas-Whatley, to come forward and go and see him and sort out this incident. Q.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why did you ask for the quick reaction force?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: The number of troops at the time, Your Honour, was increasing -- wrong, the number of HVO troops at the time was increasing. I also saw a number of RPG-7 rocket-propelled grenades which I used for anti-armour purposes being deployed. Because the number of troops was increasing, I felt that having only two Warriors there was an insufficient force to protect the convoy should violence be necessary. The position of the lead and rear Warrior was also of concern. They were not mutually supporting. Because they could not see each other, one could not cover the other in the event of an incident, and I felt that perhaps a show of force and the deployment of the steel fist as opposed to the velvet glove was beginning to become appropriate. Certainly, I was beginning to fear for my own safety, and, at one stage, I was significantly threatened by a number of the troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you took these two steps, and then did you stay at the area or did you leave?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: After a period of one or two hours, the instant began to stabilise. We achieved a stalemate. We were not going through, but they were not going to take the vehicles away from us. Once that had been achieved, I felt it was appropriate to recover myself and my team back from the area of the incident to Stara Bila to debrief the commanders there and to ensure that the appropriate liaison officer who had personal dealings with the commands in the area was deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you aware that the incident eventually resolved without loss?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Yes, I am. A compromise was arranged in which neither side lost face. The HVO were not prepared to allow the Warriors to escort the UNHCR convoy. They insisted that they should escort it and move it to a field nearby for further processing, I believe was the phrase used. We were adamant that the U.N. would remain with that convoy, there were UNHCR loads, and the drivers were under the employ of the UNHCR, although the drivers were Muslims. So the compromise was arranged that the Warriors that had escorted them as far as the checkpoint stayed where they were and did not cross the checkpoint, but we arranged for two Warriors to be on the other side of the checkpoint in such a way that the HVO had control of the convoy for a short period and were able to process them in a field but under significant scrutiny by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the time, who was commanding the regiment?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: The commanding officer was Lieutenant-Colonel Bob Stewart. However, he was away during that period, and his second in command at the time, Major Bryan Watters, was commanding the regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know what, if any, communication there was between the young officer in the Warrior and Major Watters? Do you know anything about what Major Watters may have done to negotiate the freeing up of this convoy, or were those matters outside your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Those matters were outside my knowledge. I had spoken on two occasions by means of high-frequency radio to the operations room back at Stara Bila. I did not speak with Major Watters at the time, although I did speak with him subsequently when I returned to Stara Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You will be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before that, Mr. Nice, it occurs to me that it might be helpful to have a map which covers all these troop deployments. We are now in the position of getting a considerable amount of evidence about the Serb troops and the deployment of them in the area, and now some of the RBiH forces and likewise the HVO. We need to know and be satisfied about where the front lines were, for instance, and it would be helpful if, during the recess, we could have a map, I would find it helpful to have a map which contains all the information that we have to date according to the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll attend to that. There may be two ways of doing it. One would be to synthesise all the material presently presented and put it on a single document. Another would be for an appropriate expert to set matters out and to ensure that that also reflects the evidence. I will discuss the matter this afternoon with those who can assist me, and we will attempt to meet your needs by the end of the recess. It will be helpful for us to know whether you would like it to be on a scale of map of the type that some of us have been using, the map that I first showed to the witness, which is, of course, a useful scale for reading but somewhat unwieldy, or if you would like it on a slightly smaller scale so that it's more manageable. The scale of the exhibit of the witness is, of course, exactly the same scale as the coloured map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's difficult then to see everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Because this will be a large area which is going to be covered. I mean, I have in mind, for instance, Colonel Watters' evidence, the evidence we've now got about the Jajce Brigade, and, as I said, the evidence about the various Serb forces in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Leave it with me, and I'll do the best I can. But if, for example, over the adjournment of today or tomorrow, the Court as a whole forms a view as to what size of document would most fit with its management of paperwork, I will fit in with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I should say that if the Defence wanted to provide their own account of the matter in the same way, of course, they're free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. May I begin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Major, my name is Bob Stein. I represent Dario Kordic. Now, we have two problems. You speak quickly and I speak quickly. To keep the interpreters and the reporters from jumping out of their chairs and stopping the proceedings and the Judge from appropriately cautioning me, we must go slowly, with a pause between my question and your answer and your answer and my question. Is that satisfactory to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: I'm very happy to oblige.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I want to first talk about the two HVO commanders who you told the Court were anti-Muslim. As I understand it, the name of the first commander was, again, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: I didn't give a name for either commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: What was the first commander's name?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot recall their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The anti-Muslim attitude that you talked about was determined by you in conversation with them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: It was determined on a number of factors. If we deal with the commander from Vares first --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: -- the commander had a number of dealings and a series of meetings with me where I tried to broker a moderately amicable arrangement to ensure the passage of aid from the area of Breza through Vares and north into the Tuzla salient. Those negotiations were exceptionally acrimonious and, on a number of occasions, led to the HVO commander for the area getting up and walking out when he saw who was opposite him. So the evidence there is one of physical hatred, they refused to be in the same room together, numerous conversations that I had, and the conversations I had with the Canadian liaison officer who subsequently took responsibility for the area of Visoko, Vares, Breza.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: As I understand your direct testimony, the Vares HVO commander had had friends killed by the opposing forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No. What I said was that attempts had been made on his life. To be more precise, he alleged to me that attempts had been made on his life, namely, that a car bomb had been used to kill him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That in and of itself might make you angry with your enemy, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Quite possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And the other commander was from where?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Zepce.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: As to the Zepce commander, do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No, I cannot recall his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Had you had --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I was breaking my own rule. Had you had personal contact with the commander from Zepce?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: How many occasions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: I do not recall exactly, but certainly six, ten, perhaps more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Did he also share with you the basis of his animus towards the enemy?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Again, can we agree, in wartime, it's certainly not surprising to have a hatred of your enemies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Quite possibly. As a professional soldier, I don't subscribe to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The individual from Zepce, as I recall your testimony, was not a professional soldier?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, I want to make clear, the Jajce Brigade which arrived in your operative zone, when did it arrive?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Again, I can't recall the date exactly. I didn't maintain a specific diary. I remember the incident very clearly because I took a bottle of whiskey to the local commander to say, "Hello. I'm your liaison officer." We sat down together, and about an hour after I'd arrived, the area commander or sector commander, Ganic Nehru, arrived and was surprised to see that I had beaten him there to one of his new brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Could that have been in November of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No, it could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Was that before your time of service?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No. At the time of November 1992, I was the battalion public information officer, a post I remained in until Christmas of 1992. It was only probably around the 3rd or 4th of January that I became the liaison officer for this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I neglected to ask, what were your dates of service in this particular theatre of operation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: I arrived in theatre with the main body deployment, which I gather was October/November, to the best of my memory. I deployed north about 12 hours after arriving in Split --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, let me just cut you off. Just your dates of service, start and finish.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: I went through from the beginning of the tour, arriving with the main body, to the end which was May, mid May.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: 1993, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The arrival of the Jajce Brigade, was that close to the incidents in mid April at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: It preceded the incidents at Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Two weeks, two months, can you tell us when?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: A month, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: How far was the Jajce Brigade when it came into the arena from the front line?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Which front line?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All the front lines. Why don't you just explain it to us.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: The Jajce Brigade established themselves at the school in Biljesevo. The line of confrontation between Muslim forces and Serb forces were approximately 30 kilometres to the north on the western shoulder of the Doboj salient. The line of confrontation with -- the demarcation between the zones of influence between Croats and Muslims at the time ran roughly from the Zenica junction, indicated here (indicating), along the high ground, down towards Kiseljak to the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. I want to talk about the part of your testimony relative to Mr. Kordic being nervous. As I understand, that conclusion came from two sources?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The first source was Lieutenant Maric?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Neven Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Did he tell you what his source was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: His orders came from the commander in Vares. Lieutenant Neven Maric had --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. So that's the military commander?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Correct, the military commander. Lieutenant Neven Maric had just celebrated his promotion from being a detachment of the Vares forces to becoming a fully fledged brigade commander in his own right, and he had celebrated the formation of the Kotromanic Brigade a few days earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And his source of information that Mr. Kordic was nervous was what?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. Your second source was Captain Major Whatley?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Captain at the time, Dundas-Whatley.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Not Major?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Still a Captain. Captain Whatley, what was his source of information?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Captain Dundas-Whatley was the liaison officer for this area and on numerous occasions had dealt with Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Did he specifically tell you his source of information?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, I want to talk about the trip you made on the road from Kakanj to Vitez two days before the incidents in Ahmici. Do I take it you saw no evidence on either side, that is, the HVO or the BiH, relative to preparations for an assault on Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Correct. I did not see evidence that led me to suspect an assault was about to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. Just to backtrack a tad, were you aware, of course, that the commander in Vares was Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: The name rings a bell, but to be honest, it's now seven years past, and as I'm currently involved back in the Balkans again, I'm more focused on issues like Gracko at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We won't ask you date questions or anniversary dates or embarrassing things like that, which none of us remember, I guarantee you. Let's talk about the checkpoint episode. As I gather, the best recollection you have is sometime after April 16 and before May 5?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No, sometime after April 20th and before May 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. And you pinpoint those dates how?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: The incident of Ahmici, if I recall, was the 16th?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: When the fighting started in the Lasva Valley, I normally operated in one or two unarmoured Land Rovers with the team of between three and five people, namely myself, my driver bodyguard, and my interpreter, and maybe two others as an escort. To that end, driving around in an unarmoured Land Rover when there was an awful lot of sniping and shooting going on is not a particularly healthy option.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In fact, they are called thin skins or something along those lines?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: I certainly never did. You may have an alternate source.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sorry. It was a curiosity question.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: I did make one attempt after that two or three days to drive east to find out what was happening in Kakanj. I got about two kilometres, whereupon we were engaged by sniper from the south and decided that it was a good idea to turn round.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So that's how you pinpoint the first day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. So that's your point of reference for April 20 or so, and the other point of reference?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, I was deployed to the area of Zavidovici to Tesanj, north of Tesanj, in a small pocket just to the southwest of Doboj for a period of two to three days with a Captain Mike Stanley, where we worked alongside the local headquarters in monitoring flight violations or alleged flight violations by aircraft. This was during the operation to deny airspace or military airspace to ex-JNA aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I want to talk about the incident itself. Your translator was Muslim?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: I can't remember. I did at the time. I knew at the time. To be quite honest, her religion was irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do I take it, as a general matter, that most of the translators were Muslim as opposed to Croat?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You had some Croat translators?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: We had Croat, Serb, and Muslim translators.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In this particular episode, you can't remember or tell us who the translator was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: I can recall her face and could select her from a photograph. I think, to answer your first question, I think she was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. The brigade or the local commander that you were talking to on the road, I believe you said he was a lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: He was?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: He was a lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No, I believe he was a young officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. The young officer with whom you were speaking, do you know his name --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: -- or his rank?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Do you know which brigade he was out of?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Were you actually face to face with him, having this discussion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Not over the radios?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No. It was at a range of about three feet, and at one point I had the barrel of a rifle shoved into my face to make the point that they were going to take the convoy. It was one of the reasons I recall the incident so clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. Do I take it that in essence, you said to him, "Dario Kordic has given permission for this convoy to pass"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: His response was basically to say, "No, he hasn't. He told me to stop it"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Also correct. And to elaborate, he was actually surprised when I said that Dario Kordic had given permission for the convoy to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: His immediate comeback was, "Dario told me to stop it"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Did you personally confirm, in any fashion, whether or not the statement that Kordic told him to stop the convoy was, in fact, accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No, although I said that he should phone back and confirm what the score was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do you know, of your own personal knowledge, as to whether or not that commander did just that, called back?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: I believe he did, and my recollection is that he made a phone call or, wrong, that he went away for a period into the building that was to the south, and he returned and told me that as far as he was concerned, the convoy was stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: As to whether he made a call or to whom, you can't help us?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Did you learn from any other source, intelligence, et cetera, as to whether or not Dario Kordic had, in fact, given orders to stop the convoy?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, from your experience in the theatre, were there instances in which officers from both sides of the conflict would look you straight in the eye and lie to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: While you were negotiating this episode, did you see any black-clad soldiers in or about the convoy?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Again as a result of this convoy episode, did you hear anything from BritBat that they were considering launching an armed assault on Busovaca because of this convoy being stopped?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Sorry, that BritBat would launch an armed assault on Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Exactly what I asked.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No, I have no recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do I take it from your evidence that this episode would have, in the normal course, been reported back up the chain of command through a milinfosum or some other writing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: To be honest, I'm not in a position to effectively answer that. My area of interest was not this particular area. I provided milinfo. I didn't collate or manage it, so I'm afraid that's outside my cognisance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Bad question on my part. Did you, as a result of this episode, prepare a milinfosum or some writing, whatever you call it, a report of it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No, I did not produce any written material from this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. As I understand the normal course of the way the British army in a hostile environment works is to report incidents like this up the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Yes. However, you have to understand that this particular time, I think the vernacular phrase is all hell was breaking lose. We had incidents ongoing in Srebrenica, which was where most of the world's press was focused; we had Ahmici, the investigation was still ongoing; we had significant fighting in and around Vitez. My principal effort was in stopping fighting breaking out in the area of Kakanj, where there was significant movement of heavy weapons. This was a very minor incident and, to be quite honest, was not worthy, in my opinion, of a significant report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. Consistent with that answer, when you were approached by the Office of the Prosecutor in 1995 telephonically, you were asked questions by the investigator of a variety of things, and is it fair to say, even at that point in time in 1995, this was insignificant enough that you did not mention it to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No. The conversation never touched upon it. More precisely, 1995, if I recall, I had just come off a night shift, I was pretty tired, and when someone phones you up out of the blue and asks questions, you just want to stop, finish, and go to bed. Also, to say that this was insignificant, militarily it may well have been insignificant. Personally, I remember it vividly because I've never felt more threatened in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: By the young officer?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: By a number of his troops, who made an effort to make sure I was -- or tried to make sure I was intimidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The late-night phone caller from the OTP --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Sorry, the early morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sorry. How about the interruption from the OTP investigator? Did he specifically ask you about Dario Kordic, Colonel Blaskic; did he ask you about any names?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: To be quite honest, without seeing the notes of that, I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you those notes. If you would just put that on the ELMO, please. We don't need to admit them. We can just put it on the ELMO. Take your time, Major, but I think you'll find no reference to Mr. Kordic in those notes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I must disagree. If you look about ten lines down, the last line of the first paragraph, you'll see Dario Kordic mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes. With regard to the episode of the convoy being stopped, you'll see no reference to Mr. Kordic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Again, forgive me if I disagree, but the Travnik checkpoint is nowhere near Busovaca, and this instance, although I do not recall it, cannot be one in the same. Dario Kordic's area of influence did not, I believe, cover Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Agreed. This whole witness interview apparently doesn't mention the episode about which you testified at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I have been fortunate enough to be given a statement by James Connelly, who served with you, I believe. Do you recall Captain Connelly?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Are you sure he was a captain?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sergeant.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: I believe at the time he was a staff sergeant or a sergeant in the intelligence corps. He was working in the milinfo section in Stara Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: At page 5 of his statement, he -- this is a statement to the Prosecutor -- he notes: "Checkpoints were almost invariably set up on the orders of brigade commands. These brigade commands received their orders from their senior ops group or ops zone." Would you agree with that observation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: I cannot agree nor disagree. It is outside my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. The next question, we may move on or not. He says: "The control over such military decisions would rest with the senior military commander." Agree, disagree?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Again, I can do neither. You're asking me to comment on someone else's material based on their own experience and based on knowledge which I did not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you. You've been very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, we only have a couple of very brief questions. Mr. Ellis, I'm Bozidar Kovacic, and I'm a lawyer from Rijeka, with my colleague, Mr. Mikulicic, and I represent here the defence of the accused Mario Cerkez. I shall be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the arrival of the Jajce 305th Brigade significantly disrupted the balance of forces in the area. Did I understand your meaning?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you make any assessment or did you get any assessment about the strength of those units? How many men were there when they arrived in the area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: I believe the figures were two battalions each of two or three hundred infantry, one company of military police, approximately two or three heavy mortars, 120 millimetre with limited ammunition, one or two heavy machine guns, a 12,7 Dushka (phoen), a number of 762 light machine guns, and a quantity of rifles. Heavy weapons and their ammunition were very thin, although there was adequate, I assess, quantities of small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that a unit of that strength in that part of Bosnia at that time was indeed a very strong, a very good unit, of course in comparison with some other formations, that it was a very powerful unit?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree, particularly as the Jajce Brigade had shown itself to be a very resolute and tough formation in the fighting around Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did I get you properly? You're telling us about its combat experience?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Yes. It was an experienced combat unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It belonged to the Muslim side of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned a name, Nehru Ganic, and associated him with the 305th Brigade. What duty did he discharge in it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Nehru Ganic was the operational zone commander who had under command the Jajce Brigade and the 319 Mountain Brigade, if I recall correctly, which was commanded by Dzemal Hadzic. He was certainly a very senior and significant figure in the Kakanj area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ellis, could you tell me if the commander of that unit, that is, Jajce, the 305th Brigade, if Rifat Planincic was also one of the commanding officers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Perhaps I -- Rifat Planincic. Does that name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: The name Rifat Planincic does not -- I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The name of Mensur Kelestura, does it mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No, I do not recall that name either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Let us move on to another subject. You told us and we heard a great many detail about the convoy that was intercepted and all the negotiations in this relation, and then you said that when the situation calmed down somewhat, that from that place where it was blocked, you started back to Stara Bila and you then entered the municipality of Vitez, if you knew where the boundaries of municipalities were at the time. So on that part of the road next to Stara Bila, did any HVO unit patrol or any troops, did they stop you, did they try to block your way or anything?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No. No HVO troops tried to block me entering the opstina of Stara Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It was not your area of responsibility, but you nevertheless used to go there, Stara Bila. Was Stara Bila in the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Again, I will agree with you for lack of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (In English) Fair enough. (Interpretation) You also spoke about the events a few days after the Ahmici conflict. At that time, I assume you gathered information about the developments, so would you remember if in Zenica, and it should have happened on the 20th of April, if in Zenica an agreement had been reached that the road control should be run jointly by civilian and military police, and did you ever see such checkpoints with combined civilian and military police after the 20th of April?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: First of all, the area of Zenica was not in my area of responsibility. Therefore, any agreements that were reached there I was not present or immediately privy to. However, a joint military/civil checkpoint was established, and if I indicate on the map, at that location (indicating) at the junction between the road to Zenica and the road to Kakanj is the point where a joint checkpoint between both HVO an ABiH was established with both military and civil representatives, basically on the autoput where the bridge had been blown out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now could you tell me, please, Major Ellis, if you ever met Mario Cerkez in your contacts with the HVO, Mario Cerkez who is my client?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Not that I recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You do not know him?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Not that I recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you very much. Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Three things, please, Major Ellis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your interpreter, did she ever give you cause for concern about the reliability of her interpreting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was being an interpreter a paid job?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Yes. Furthermore, all our interpreters were required to wear a British army uniform so that they could not be accused of any bias. We also brought them within the military community to further strengthen political/social bonding, that they are identified with the U.N. more closely than they are identified with any faction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Second, in the course of the discussions at the convoy, was any other name of authority, apart from Kordic's, mentioned at any stage?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Third, in relation to the convoy, was it stopped at a checkpoint or merely at a point on a road?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: At that period in Bosnia, a checkpoint was any point on a road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the troops present, the HVO troops present, did they make this a checkpoint in any formal way?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: No. Normally a checkpoint, in the formal sense, would have a chicane made up of metal knife rests, normally interspersed with barbed wire. Anti-tank mines, either TMA 3s or TMA 4s, would be laid. Quite frequently, the anti-tank mines would be used like traffic cones, which made life very interesting at night. There would normally be a stop sign. Certainly the more formally-established checkpoints, such as the junction in Travnik or what I've referred to as the Zenica junction, the Zenica fly-over here indicated on the map, and defensive positions would be constructed. None of that was present at the instant that is being referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was any traffic being allowed to pass in the contrary direction or not, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: The only traffic that was allowed to pass were the three journalist vehicles which I negotiated their way through.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Although that concludes what I need to ask about the questions you've been asked, is it the case that you are able to pinpoint this date, if any of us need it further pinpointed, because there is a newspaper article?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: There is a newspaper article which was written by the journalist Tom Coughlin. The date, I believe, is also exactly recorded by an officer who has already given evidence to this Tribunal, a major currently, Mike Dooley, who is serving with 17 (phoen) Brigade headquarters in Pristina, and he informed me before I came out, came back to The Hague, that from his diaries from the time, he would be able to pinpoint it exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. The newspaper article was written by one of the journalists who you'd helped?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think the content of the article inflamed you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Tom Coughlin was looking for a good story. He needed a story. To that end, it was dramatised. Like all good stories, it had a grain of truth at its heart and was very hard to deny in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What newspaper was it published in, did you tell us?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ELLIS
utterances.text: Either the Sunday Telegraph or the Sunday Times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have nothing else for this witness. I know that researches have so far not identified a milinfosum or other document that would give the date precisely. I would ask that he be released, subject to any further questions of the Court, but that he stay behind until I satisfy myself that there's no document that I can serve on the Defence today before he leaves The Hague and in respect of which they might wish to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No doubt that can be sorted out today. Major, as far as the Court is concerned, you are released. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. You can go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We are in a position to carry on with Mr. Akhavan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is possibly a convenient moment, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's a tiny matter of detail that I promised I would sort out at the end of last week when the Court was running short of time, and I ought perhaps just to check has been dealt with. It relates to Prosecution Exhibit 27/2 -- I'm so sorry, Defence Exhibit 27/2. I believe improved copies of an original were distributed, and if not, they should now be made available. The Tribunal will recall that the document in its original condition had come from the original confirming materials, as I think counsel explained, but the notes on the bottom left-hand side were substantially illegible. I sent out to get or tried to get a better original and was successful. The footnotes include, under footnote 2, "Known as Jokeri (Black Knights), under direct control of HDZ (Dario Kordic) and local control of Comd 1 OG."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a BritBat document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's right, yes. I'm sorry it wasn't available earlier in this precise form, but it is now available, and there it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, Mr. Akhavan is coming back after the adjournment. How much longer do you anticipate being with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I would think, Your Honour, that we could be all or a substantial part of the day. We were actually delivered about over 50 pages of notes and a draft report that had been prepared by Mr. Akhavan, and suffice it to say, they raise some matters that need to be drawn to the attention of the Trial Chamber in meticulous detail because they throw considerable light upon the very broad conclusions and opinions that he expressed during his direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Bear in mind we're adjourning at 1.00 today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That being the case, Your Honour, I would think that we would probably take the rest of today and perhaps an hour or, at most, two hours tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, since you are asking for planning purposes, I would also like to inform you that probably I will need -- it, of course, depends on how many questions will be asked by the other Defence -- but probably at least an hour and a half, two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just add a small explanation related to what my colleague, Mr. Nice, said? Indeed, we have received this paper as a part of the supporting material. That is clear from the written number on the top of the document which was used on the copy we produced. I don't see it on this document, because the registrar was numerating all the papers with their numbers, being letter D and then the number. According to the title with small letters above the main title of the document, which reads "U.N. restricted," it is my opinion -- of course, I cannot claim -- that the source is not the British Battalion but other UNPROFOR bodies. Some other documents which we have seen which were issued by BritBat usually do not use the word "UNPROFOR". They are using "British Battalion" or something else, a specific unit or something. So I think since this material was originally offered in supporting material by the Prosecution, it is up to them to tell us exactly what is the source of this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, no doubt you can deal with that in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In due course. I'm more concerned immediately about the timetable. First of all, there's been quite extensive cross-examination of Mr. Akhavan so far, without any clear case being put to him, and there does come a limit to the amount of time that can properly be spent on simply general examination. Second, more materially, in order to ensure that we have a week well used for helpful evidence, I have secured the attendance tonight for tomorrow morning of General Cordy-Simpson, and although no particular privileges should be afforded to rank, I'd prefer not to keep him hanging around, and I would be particularly embarrassed if I was obliged to ask him to come back for cross-examination on a later date. I think he's happy enough to stay over tonight, not only tonight but tomorrow night, until Thursday morning or Thursday, but it would be helpful to have an accurate forecast of the time required in cross-examination so that we can either decide necessary to apply to interpose him again in Akhavan's evidence; alternatively, to take Akhavan to the conclusion and then take the General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long do you anticipate he's going to take in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm reducing the time, I think, all the time. It's unlikely to be more than two hours, probably between one and two, I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. To be fair to the Defence, you say that a considerable amount of time has been spent on the cross-examination. In fact, it's an hour and twenty minutes, which, I'm afraid, by our standards is not a long time. Mr. Sayers, it's obviously important, if possible, that we try and finish both of these witnesses this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I fully appreciate, and I absolutely don't want to inconvenience Lieutenant-General Cordy-Simpson. We're more than happy to take him or allow the Prosecution to put his evidence on tomorrow, if they wish to do so, and to complete his evidence tomorrow. Of course, it's difficult to predict without hearing the witness, but I would not anticipate that our cross-examination would last more than an hour for the Lieutenant-General. Then we could perhaps finish with Mr. Akhavan on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Although it's inconvenient for Mr. Akhavan, he is here. The General is not. Therefore, we will interpose him tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like today to start by marking the notes and the draft report that were delivered to us yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D65/1 and D66/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, we will take a break for the interpreters in an hour's time, about five or ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, would you identify the document that was marked as, I believe, Exhibit D65/1?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: You refer to the document which is presently on the video, marked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you mean the notes or the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The notes.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: 2943.1, those are the handwritten notes which I took during my mission to the Lasva Valley region in May of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I think you are referring to Exhibit D65/1, and these notes were made contemporaneously during your one-week visit to the Lasva Valley; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then the second document, D66/1, I believe, is a draft report that you authored --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- connected with the results of your visit?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct. It's a preliminary draft.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Would it be fair to say that these documents were never produced in the Blaskic case or in the Kupreskic case?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: These documents were not found until after the Blaskic case, but I do believe actually that they were found by the U.N. Centre for Human Rights only recently. We'd requested these documents, I recall, about a year --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, the question was simple. We'll be able to speed up the examination if you answer the question rather than going off into discussive explanations. Is it true that these notes and the draft report were not produced in the Blaskic case and they were not produced in the Kupreskic case?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were requested but not available, so they were not produced, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to go through some of these notes with you. Would it be fair to say that the first section of these notes deal with the briefing that you were given by various members of BritBat?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: On the first page, you have the name "Dario Kordic from Busovaca." The phrase "Local HVO commander" is scratched out, and it says "HDZ leader, second in command from Boban"; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were never, in fact, told that Dario Kordic was an HVO leader, were you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was told that the HDZ and the HVO have an inextricable relation with one another, not that Dario Kordic is necessarily a military commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm answering your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- it was a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with the question.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was not told that he was an HVO military commander, but I was told that the HDZ and HVO had really an inseparable chain of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is there any reference to that in your notes?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe it may be somewhere within these notes. If not, it was based on the general recollection I have of what I was told about the situation in the region. Not everything is in these notes. Most things are in these notes, mainly details which I needed to remember for the drafting of the report. But I do believe that later in the report, I do refer to the facts, on several occasions, that Dario Kordic gave political direction to the HVO in the region, which meant that even if he was not involved in having some sort of tactical operational command of the military, he was giving overall direction to the military in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it's somewhere in the notes. I can find it for you. It may take a little bit of time. I just reviewed it a few minutes ago. They were members of the British Battalion, to the best of my recollection, and on more than one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I've taken the liberty of numbering these notes. If you would just turn to page 34, these notes detail your meeting with Mr. Kordic on May the 5th?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. It's not in that area where I have the notes which I refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He told you that he was the vice-president of Herceg-Bosna, I believe.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He also told you that he was the vice-president of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, I would like to go through --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: And there is HDZ political support of HVO, so even by his own admission, he did indicate that the HDZ gave political direction to the HVO. But I was told, as I said. We could -- possibly during the recess, I could find the exact statements of various British Battalion members who clearly indicated Dario Kordic was the man in control, not necessarily in the sense that he had day-to-day military command but that he was the one who was calling the shots, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Really? Who was the BritBat liaison officer responsible for the Busovaca area?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Does the name Captain Matthew Dundas-Whatley sound familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. He accompanied me, I believe, during much of my visit to the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He was the liaison officer, was he not?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It sounds reasonable to assume that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He arranged your meetings with Colonel Blaskic and Mario Cerkez on May the 4th, 1993, did he not?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and I believe he was also responsible for arranging the meeting with Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your meeting with Dario Kordic was rather short and abrupt, wasn't it, sir? About 15 minutes, I believe.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We'll get into that in due course. Let me begin my questions today with the first visit that you paid to the village of Ahmici on May the 1st, 1993. I believe that you accompanied Lieutenant Colonel Stewart and his soon-to-be successor, Lieutenant-Colonel Alistair Duncan.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The 1st Cheshires were rotating out of their area of responsibility, and the Prince of Wales Own Regiment was rotating in to take over the responsibilities of 1st Cheshire at about the time that you were there; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: During the time that you drove out to Ahmici, you actually saw houses on fire, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: As I had mentioned the other day, during the evening that we arrived to Vitez, we saw houses actually being put on fire as we were in the tank, and when we were in Ahmici on the first day, I don't recall seeing houses being put on fire, no. There were some houses which were still smouldering, but the houses which we saw being put on fire were in the evening when we arrived. Subsequently in one of the days, we saw homes being put on fire in neighbouring hamlets and villages. I don't recall the exact date, but that was not Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me read to you a sentence from your statement dated June the 23rd, 1995, and which you signed a few years later. "I arrived in Vitez on the evening of 30 April 1993. I was brought to Vitez by a BritBat Warrior from Kiseljak. I was first taken into Vitez because BritBat had seen some houses on fire. I could see, through a small portal in the Warrior, that some houses were burning." Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly what I referred to just a moment ago. The first evening when we arrived, we saw homes which had been set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in relation to the evidence that we covered yesterday, I suppose, and the collection of bodies that were placed by the cemetery in Ahmici by BritBat, you did, did you not, sir, have the opportunity to receive an extensive briefing from then Lieutenant Michael Dooley?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, you mentioned the name yesterday. It sounded familiar, and upon review of my notes, I recall that he indeed did give us a briefing, along with other members of the British Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Indeed, on page 11 of your notes, there's one reference to a conversation with Lieutenant Dooley?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
