utterances.text: Page 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it's page 10. Correct. It says, "Witnessed HVO forces cleansing houses with grenades and spraying bullets." That's the reference that you're speaking of?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Also on page 16, there was a second conversation that you apparently had with Lieutenant Dooley?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is the page on top of which it says "Ahmici not a defended village"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No, it's the page that says, "Lieutenant Mike Dooley," underlined twice.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Did Lieutenant Dooley relate to you the fact that he personally had made four trips in his armoured fighting vehicle to Ahmici on April the 16th and that he had actually collected approximately 24 bodies?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Towards the bottom of that page, you will see my notes, where he says that he arrived in the early afternoon of 16 April, where "Ahmici" is circled, and he explains his observations, the presence of HVO soldiers, some sort of residual resistance of Muslim civilians defending themselves with shotguns, that he discovered many bodies, most without shoes, suggesting that they may have fled their home without much warning or that it would have been so early in the morning that many were still asleep or at their home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did Lieutenant Dooley tell you that other armoured units had preceded him into Ahmici that morning, commanded by Lieutenant Monty Wooley?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall. I may even have elsewhere in my notes some information to the effect that others had visited Ahmici as well, so I do remember that I spoke with more than one member of the British Battalion who had visited Ahmici on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recall Lieutenants Dooley and Wooley telling you that they performed this body collection exercise under intense fire in the middle of an active firefight?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall one way or the other, and I'm not sure what relevance it would have had for our purposes. What I have here is that they did pick up 10 to 20 bodies and that there was still some fighting going on. I'm not sure whether your characterisation of intense gunfire would be accurate. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: -- indication which we were given is that by the time they arrived, much of the killing had already been done. Obviously, bodies were lying around in the village, so it's fair to assume that much of the fighting had been done already.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Let me just read you a portion of Lieutenant Dooley's November 1996 statement. "The area where we collected these bodies was under intense fire. Tracer fire was being fired over us, and houses were burning everywhere." Does that refresh your recollection on the subject of whether there was an active firefight in progress at the time that the British forces were actually collecting bodies in Ahmici, sir?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, well, as I said, the notes right here in front of you indicate that there was still gunfire going on. So, yes, it refreshes my memory from just 30 seconds ago when we discussed these notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I believe that you actually personally inspected not just one depression or trench where you discovered spent shell casings of undetermined calibre, but actually you saw four or five depressions or ditches where there were agglomerations of spent shell casings. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: In relation to these so-called killing fields or in general? In relation to that particular area where some 20 bodies had been discovered, I only recall looking at one depression. It may have been that the depression consisted of further depressions, but I only recognised one general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, as I understand it, your second visit to Ahmici occurred on the next day, May the 2nd.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You proceeded to Ahmici under armed guard; right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your colleague, Mr. Osorio, was with you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When you refer, in your draft report, to a team from the U.N. Centre for Human Rights visiting the area, actually you mean you and Mr. Osorio, don't you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The standard term that was used was "a team."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you say that you tried to speak to an elderly Croat lady who was in a house?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: She was not in a house. She was walking with two younger children.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: She told you that she actually knew nothing about who had been fighting in the village or who had killed the villagers, did she not?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: She did not tell me. She told my colleague, Thomas, because I could not speak Serbo-Croatian. He approached her with the aim, as we had discussed earlier, of trying to see if those who were still in the village could tell us anything about the events of that day. She obviously was very fearful of speaking with us, and she simply said that, "I don't know anything." I could even remember her shaking her head, meaning to say -- saying, "No, I don't know anything, I cannot tell you anything."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, in your December 1994 statement, you say that this old lady "said that she knew nothing about who had destroyed the village and killed the people"?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after your second visit to the village of Ahmici, I believe that you made a visit to the city of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It would have been on May the 3rd, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This was a city under the control of Muslim forces; right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Under the control of Bosnian government forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It was also the headquarters of the centre of Muslim forces in the region, the 3rd Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You visited, I believe, the Bosnian Institute for War Crimes, did you not?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As a result of that visit, you were directed towards approximately 100 to 150 survivors from the village of Ahmici; right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All women and children; right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Plus some elderly, but predominantly women and children, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: They informed you that they had been detained at a school facility in the village of Dubravica, right, --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- and that they had not been mistreated at all?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Some of them indicated they had been there. I recall others had simply fled and who had been hiding in the forest or otherwise had escaped the region. And I'm not sure if the characterisation is correct to say that all of them said that they were not mistreated. From what I recall vaguely, and I'm not even sure if this was something we took down in our notes, but I believe that the people were fed and they were kept in reasonably good conditions. But we do recall in one case people suggesting that a woman had been raped, for example, that some people had been beaten. What is good or bad under the conditions prevailing in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time is a relative concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You decided that your colleague, Mr. Osorio, would return the next day to interview those people, given his foreign language skills; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not only because of his foreign language skills but as a sort of division of labour, I would meet with the HVO leaders in the region and he would speak with more of the witnesses in order to further corroborate their allegations as to what had transpired in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When you were present in Zenica at the facility to which you were directed by the Institute for War Crimes, did you take the opportunity to attempt to interview people yourself?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Myself personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was not in a position to without a translator, which is why Thomas Osorio, my colleague, took the lead there. But, yes, we did take care to actually speak to some of the people without the presence of others, both because we did not want the discussions to be controlled, if you like, by members of the Institute for War Crimes or others, and, secondly, because we wanted to see if people are giving consistent accounts of events without hearing each other's stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You actually did get consistent accounts from the people that you spoke to at least, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: For example, they told you a uniform story about soldiers in regular camouflage uniforms and HVO patches who had participated in the attack in the morning of the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct, and in many cases, they named soldiers whom they happened to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Not a single person told you that they had spotted someone in a black uniform in the village of Ahmici that morning, did they, sir?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall anyone saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know, I believe you may have given us some testimony about this already, but did you know that there are some 300 Croat civilians actually in the gaol in Zenica while you were there?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: We discussed that yesterday. We did know that there was a general harassment of Croats in Zenica, and this was reflected in our report. I don't know whether the specific facts of people being detained was reflected, but we were aware that there were difficult situations, and this was related to me by Colonel Blaskic and others, as you see from the handwritten notes which I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that there was a separate detention facility for captured Croat combatants located at the music school in Zenica and run under the auspices of the 7th Muslim Brigade, sir?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: We had heard something to that effect, but I have only a vague recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were actually given some briefing on the nature of this military unit, the 7th Muslim Brigade, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, among others by Colonel Blaskic, I believe, according to my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And also by BritBat, if you take a look at page 3?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, by BritBat as well, yes, "7th Muslim Brigade, local people who are religious fundamentalists."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that the brigade contained foreign agents, about 100 to 150 of them, of mixed origin, Saudi and Iranian, and that the 7th Muslim Brigade answers directly to Zenica and not to locals or local commanders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know whether the institution that you visited, the Institute for War Crimes, whether that was an agency of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that officially it was an independent organisation, but I think most of us realised that it is very closely associated with the government. Therefore, we did approach them with some degree of caution, as I indicated earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with an institution called The Centre for the Documentation of Genocide and War Crimes in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you visit that facility as well, sir, while you were there?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I'm not sure if these two are the same institution or not, but we only visited one institution, where we were told by the British Battalion that we would be able to locate survivors from Ahmici, and that was our sole purpose for approaching them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you make any notes of your interviews with people who had actually lived through the events at Ahmici on the morning of April the 16th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that those notes were mostly taken by my colleague, Thomas Osorio, although I listened in on --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you take any notes?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't believe so. It could be that I have -- I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Then, as I understand it, the next thing that you did was return to the Vitez area and request the assistance of BritBat liaison officers to arrange various interviews for you, and the people that you interviewed on the Croat side were, let me see if I've got them right and in order, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic; right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who was subsequently indicted by this Tribunal; right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The next person was Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Also subsequently indicted by this Tribunal; right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then finally, Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As we know, subsequently indicted by this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Did you happen to interview any Croat soldiers who had participated in the events of April the 16th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, if you consider Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Cerkez soldiers, yes, I did. But if you're speaking about their subordinates, no, I did not, but the opportunity was given to the HVO commanders in the region to present us with any evidence or testimony which they wished, and they chose not to offer us anything, beyond the meeting with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ask Colonel Blaskic or Mr. Cerkez to speak with any of the soldiers who had actually participated in the fighting in that village or in the entire Lasva Valley that day?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Indeed, yes, we asked them to investigate the matter thoroughly, so I suppose that would involve speaking with those who had been involved in order to discover what had happened on that day. I don't see what --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, it's a very simple question: Did you ask for their permission to interview any foot soldiers, regular units, that were involved in hostilities throughout the Lasva Valley on the 16th of April, 1993 or not; "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. In fact, you didn't interview a single foot soldier, infantryman, artilleryman, whatever, who may have participated in the hostilities on that day, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, because under the circumstances, it was virtually impossible. Actually, the day before I met the HVO commanders, a couple of snipers tried to kill my colleague and I. Under the circumstances, I think it's understandable that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please? Could you slow down for the interpreters? Could you slow down, please, for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You didn't speak to any soldiers, infantrymen, at all as you were coming up with your conclusions; right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not the subordinates of Cerkez and Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And Blaskic and Cerkez told you that they themselves were not sure of what had gone on in Ahmici that day, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's what they said. We did, of course, when we were in Ahmici, try to approach the locals, as I recall, whichever locals we happened to see, and the result of our approaching the locals was an attempt by snipers to kill us. So I don't think it's accurate to say that we did not make a serious effort to try and speak to the inhabitants of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. Let's put it this way: You were reliant, indeed, dependent for your conclusions regarding the hostilities that day from accounts that you had received from essentially two sources: First, the Muslim survivors; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Second, the British soldiers who had been in the middle of a vigorous fire fight that day.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: And, thirdly, the physical evidence which was available in the village of Ahmici and environs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Before coming to testify today, have you reviewed any documents at all related to the events at Ahmici, other than your notes and your draft report?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you take the opportunity to interview any Croat residents of the town of Vitez, sir, to try to determine what had gone on in that town on April the 16th of 1993 and thereafter?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: All of our contacts were through the Bosnian Croat authorities of the region, and we assumed that they would be in a position to direct us if they felt that it would be necessary. We did not approach the local inhabitants without going through the local Bosnian Croat authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The answer to the question, though, is that you did not interview any Croat residents of the town of Vitez at any time during your one-week tour through the Lasva Valley; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the same holds true, I gather, for the villages of Kruscica, Poculica, Gacice, Bukve, and Donja Veceriska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, except that some of those villages that you mentioned were actually, I believe, with Sergeant Major Beck, as a group of local Croats jumped in their cars, went to the villages, and we could actually see homes being set on fire a few minutes later. So in certain cases, we --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Once again, Mr. Akhavan --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: -- could see what the locals were up to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- the answer to the question was, quite apart from the comments that you wish to interject, that you did not speak to a single resident of any of the villages that I enumerated; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but we did speak to villagers, for example, in Miletici and other places where Croats had been killed. So we did speak with local Croats. I'm not sure if it was in the particular villages that you mentioned, but I think it depended on the circumstances. We did speak with local Croats. I think it's inaccurate to say we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You say you spoke with local Croats in the village of Miletici. Were there any local Croats left in the village of Miletici?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there were. The Croats were considering leaving because they were obviously fearful, understandably, but the only people that had been killed were, I believe, the four or five young men who had been tortured and killed by local Muslims, whose homes we could actually see from some distance, from the hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me read to you an entry from milinfosum number 177, dated April the 25th, 1993, from BritBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we have a copy, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I have a copy of the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I actually don't have a copy with me, I didn't want to burden the record with any more paper, but I'm happy to make a copy at the break, and we will resume this subject when a copy is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Taking it up chronologically, Mr. Akhavan, the first meeting that you had was on May the 4th, 1993, at 11.00 a.m. with Colonel Tihomir Blaskic; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This was the first time that you had met Colonel Blaskic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the tenure of that meeting was relatively accusatorial on your part?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that parts of it were accusatorial. The first half of the meeting, as reflected by the notes, was an information session where Colonel Blaskic explained to me what the geography of the region was, what the structure of his command was, what were the forces under his command, so on and so forth. When we began to discuss the events in Ahmici, yes, I did specifically ask him who was responsible, and when he gave me what I believed were evasive answers, I became, I think, a bit firm in order to try and tell him that I did not believe his explanations were being respectful of my time and our discussion. I don't think the entire meeting was accusatorial. That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So you turned up at this meeting, and your opinion was, I think, to use the verb used in your 1995 statement, that Colonel Blaskic feigned not knowing anything about what had occurred in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that the explanations he gave were quite incredulous and, in fact, inconsistent with his own earlier statements, where, for example, he said that he is in complete control of the region and that no significant military operation takes place without his orders, but then subsequently, he suggested that elements of HOS or Mujahedin or other extremists had engaged in what was evidently a large-scale military operation and that he had no knowledge about that, and a number of other things which he said suggested that he was not dealing with me in an honest fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You told him that, upon this, your first meeting, you didn't believe him; right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I was very honest, and I said, "I'm not convinced by that explanation." Of course, prior to that meeting, I already had accumulated considerable evidence as to what had transpired.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You actually lost your temper and started shouting at Colonel Blaskic in that meeting, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure if "shouting" is correct. He did behave in an intimidating fashion, and I was not about to allow him to intimidate me. But I don't believe "shouting" is -- depending on what your standard is, of course -- the correct description.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Here is Colonel Blaskic's version of your interview in testimony he gave in the Blaskic case on the 16th of March, 1999. He says: A During the day of the 4th and the 5th, I also had a meeting with Mr. Akhavan, and he wanted me to tell him what had happened on the 16th of April, 1993, and briefly, I described the events of the 16th of April, 1993. After I briefly described the events, Mr. Akhavan said: "Your units on your orders carried out the massacre in Ahmici and killed civilians." My answer to Mr. Akhavan was that they hadn't committed a crime under my orders because I hadn't ordered the commission of a crime, and I know for certain that my units had not done that. Then he goes on to say, on page 19185 of the transcript, in response to this question: Q So Mr. Payam Akhavan appeared from somewhere. You don't know who he is. What happens then? What did he say to you and what did you say? A He was very angry after that. He started shouting: "Ahmici was in your area of responsibility." He kept repeating this, and he was perhaps irritated. I answered: "Yes, Ahmici is in my zone of responsibility. It is also in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps." I told him that there was a conflict, and after that, the meeting ended. Is that consistent with your recollection of your meeting with Colonel Blaskic that day or on those days, sir?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it's not. I think it's quite a distorted description of the events. If you would like, I can clarify and explain to you how I saw the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely, please.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I don't think Colonel Blaskic gave me a brief description, as he said it. Well, he gave me the description in the sense that there was some sort of hostilities in the region between Muslims and Croats. He gave no satisfactory description or explanation as to what had transpired in the region, in terms of atrocities committed against Muslim civilians. Secondly, I do not recall ever suggesting to him that he had ordered the acts in question. And in terms of being very angry, shouting, irritated, I, as I said, don't believe that that was the case. I did become irritated, that is true, because after two hours of evasive answers, I realised that we're not going to get anywhere. I must say that the explanation that -- as this is reflected in my notes -- that extremist elements not under his control, including either HOS, which he earlier had said is a completely insignificant force in the region, or Mujahedin themselves, had massacred the Muslims seemed almost an insulting explanation, and I don't believe, based on his demeanour or disposition or that of his colleagues in the room, that any of them were actually serious about the explanation which they were giving. You see from my notes that he said to me he never gave orders to attack civilians. My response to him is that that is not the issue here. The issue is if his soldiers were indeed responsible, even after the fact, he's responsible for taking action in order to ensure that it does not happen again. So I think my notes speak for themselves in terms of the content of what we spoke about, so, with respect, I would differ in my perception of the exchange which we had on that day, which lasted, I believe, some two, possibly three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You told him, sir, that as the commander of the HVO armed forces, he was responsible to conduct a full investigation and to identify the perpetrators of the events at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, he's given evidence to that effect. There's no need to repeat it. Is it challenged that Colonel Blaskic replied in the way in which the witness has said he did?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Evidently by Colonel Blaskic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, not Colonel Blaskic, by you. You're conducting this case. Now, is that in dispute or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is it suggested that Colonel Blaskic said?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It is suggested that Colonel Blaskic said what he said he said in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, put it to the witness properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, I put it to you, isn't it true that Colonel Blaskic actually said what he said he said in the Blaskic case a few months ago as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can't put it in that way. The witness wasn't there. What is it suggested, so that we may all know, that Colonel Blaskic said to the witness? Now, tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, isn't it true that Colonel Blaskic told you that the units under his control had not committed a crime under his orders because he had not ordered the commission of a crime and he knew for certain that his units had not perpetrated the crime?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Isn't it true that you did get angry with Colonel Blaskic and exhibited that anger in a visible fashion to him?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Isn't it true that you started shouting at him that Ahmici was in his area of responsibility and that you kept on repeating it?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not shout at him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Isn't it true that Colonel Blaskic told you that Ahmici was in his zone of responsibility, --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- and that it was also in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- and that there was a conflict?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but he did say that he had control and not the 3rd Corps. It was in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, but the HVO was in control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Isn't it also true that after that acrimonious exchange, the meeting ended?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Acrimonious, with qualifications which I had earlier mentioned, yes, the meeting ended. But the meeting went on for two or three hours, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now, who else was at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that Dundas-Whatley possibly was present at that meeting. There would have been one or two UNPROFOR translators. On the side of Colonel Blaskic, I believe there were other members of the HVO present. I believe somewhere in the middle of the meeting, a gentleman by the name of Anto Valenta, to the best of my recollection, also appeared and made a brief appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, were you told that Colonel Blaskic had already invited the creation of an investigating commission pursuant to a letter that he had sent to Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart on April the 23rd, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I actually reviewed my notes, as you had mentioned a Busovaca commission earlier. What I do recall is that on April 25th, there was a joint statement made by Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban in which they denounced all acts of ethnic cleansing, and they agreed to set up an international -- independent international commission to look into these allegations. It could be that reference was made to that during the meeting. I don't have any notes of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No, I think that you're confusing the document I'm referring to. Why don't we, just before the break, if I may, ask you to take a look at two documents, D63/1 and D64/1. Turning your attention to the first document, dated April the 22nd, 1993, have you ever seen a copy of this letter from Lieutenant Colonel Stewart to Colonel Blaskic before?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, but it is consistent with what Bob Stewart told me, that he had communicated this information to Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart tell you that he had actually requested the assistance of Colonel Blaskic in ordering an investigation into the sacking of the village?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it was clear that Bob Stewart was, both in the case of Blaskic and Cerkez, telling them the same thing that I had said, that they must investigate the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart tell you what the response to that letter was, sir?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't recall what the response was, but I don't believe that there was any sense, during my discussions with him or others, that there was a serious effort to investigate or to bring anyone to account.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would you take a look at Exhibit D64/1, sir. Were you aware --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- that Colonel Blaskic had suggested the creation of a joint commission consisting of BritBat representatives, Croat representatives, and Muslim representatives to investigate the incidents at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I recall that being mentioned during the meeting, but I don't believe that the sole purpose was to investigate the events in Ahmici. I believe it was a broader confidence-building exercise, if you like, to stabilise the situation in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just read you the very first sentence, if I may. "I am ready to send immediately the investigating commission to the village of Ahmici as well as to all other places that need to be investigated because of gathering facts about all the innocent victims in this conflict."

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, except that the date of this letter is April 23rd, and some ten days later, when I was interviewing Colonel Blaskic, unless he, out of a sense of modesty, did not want to tell me that such an investigation had actually been commenced, did not mention anything about an investigation being initiated, and I specifically asked him that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What, if anything, did Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart tell you about the suggestion to form this joint investigative commission and the progress that had been made towards forming it?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't believe any significant progress had been made. I discussed with Colonel Stewart the general matter of pressuring the local HVO commanders to investigate the matter. He was not satisfied that there was any serious intent to do so at that point in time, and I think that in retrospect, his observation was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did Major Watters ever inform you that the reason this commission was not been formed was because of a reluctance by the Muslim side to participate in such a commission and that they viewed such a commission as futile?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do believe that I actually spoke with some of the Bosnian government or, as you would say, Muslim commanders, and this is in my notes as well. I don't believe any of them trusted the HVO or any of them believed that anything would ever come out of such an investigation. But I think there was a general tension in the region at that point between the Bosnian government and Bosnian Croat forces which hampered cooperation not only in this area but in really any range of areas, including freedom of movement in the region and ceasefire and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that Colonel Blaskic had actually initiated an investigation on the side of the Bosnian Croats himself in the absence of the formation of this joint investigation commission that he had suggested?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, he certainly did not mention anything during our meeting, and I think he had, during the two or three hours, ample opportunity to do so. My impression, once again in retrospect, is that nothing really came out of the investigation, unless you're privy to certain information that I'm not. No one was named, no one was prosecuted, and the atrocities continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The final question along these lines, you actually told Colonel Blaskic, at the end of your interview, that if he did not order an investigation, then he would be seen as an accomplice; right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: In a general sense, I said that he bears responsibility for ensuring that such allegations are fully investigated and, if necessary, prosecuted. But obviously I was not in any position to tell him that I would hold him or even an institution that I was directly associated with would hold him accountable. So it was a general reminder to him of his obligations under international law as part of the preventive function of Mr. Mazowiecki's mandate as Human Rights Special Rapporteur.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That would be a convenient moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, do I take it that it's your view, consistent with what you told Colonel Blaskic during your exchange on May the 4th, 1993, that he fell down in his responsibility somehow under international law in failing to order an investigation of the events of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Based on the limited information available to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if I might just draw your attention to the next document, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D67/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, I would like you to take a look at this exhibit, which represents an order on Colonel Blaskic's part, dated May the 10th, 1993, directed to the SIS, I believe, to conduct an investigation into the events in the village of Ahmici. Have you ever seen a copy of this order before?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is it true that you have been unaware, during the last five years that you have worked for the Office of the Prosecutor, that this document was actually issued by Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: During the past five years that I've worked with the Office of the Prosecutor, I've consciously not been involved in the investigation relating to the Blaskic case, so it doesn't surprise me that I'm unaware of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say then that you see this document for the first time today?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe this document is dated six days after your meeting with Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a few final questions in so far as Colonel Blaskic is concerned. First, Colonel Blaskic consistently emphasised to you that he was in command of all military units in the HVO in Central Bosnia, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's also true, and I think that your notes reflect this, that throughout your interview with Colonel Blaskic, he never once mentioned the name Dario Kordic to you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do believe that the name of Dario Kordic may have come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In what context, sir?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but usually when I met with the individuals in question, I would review the information which had been given to me by others in terms of the structure of authority in the Lasva Valley region, and I do recall in most cases reviewing what I had earlier been told by members of the British Battalion to see whether I would receive any contrary information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic never contended that he was subordinate to Mr. Kordic in the military chain of command, did he, sir?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the military chain of command, I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. During the course of your investigation, sir, I believe that you put together a list of 18 people whom you considered to have been among the perpetrators of the events in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993; would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: My colleague, Thomas Osorio, put that list together based on the interviews he had in Zenica on the day when I was in Vitez interviewing Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Cerkez and Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say then that before you left the Lasva Valley on May the 7th, you actually had a list of suspects; right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Indeed, that list of suspects was forwarded to a commission of experts for potential prosecutions of war crimes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was submitted to the commission of experts for the purpose of their general data bank and reports. At that point in time, the mandate of the commission of experts did not extend to criminal prosecutions. Obviously, it was not a jurisdiction as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This list of suspects was never provided to the HVO, to Colonel Blaskic, or anyone else within the HVO, was it?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, and I think that that was probably a deliberate decision. We were not responsible for conducting criminal investigations, and the only reason that we took those 18 names down, in addition to the fact that it gave credibility to the statements of many of the witnesses for the purposes of our report, was simply to assist the commission. We happened to get these names, and we exceptionally decided to forward this to the commission for their purposes, to see whether they wished to follow up. But it was not our practice to conduct investigations and then to give the names to the local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, it was a very simple question: You never gave the list of suspects to the HVO, did you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I was not involved in subsequent missions to the region, so I'm not aware of what may have transpired, either on the part of our commission or the commission of experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, this was a decision that you and Colonel Stewart actually reached, isn't that true, not to turn over the names of the suspects of the --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't believe Colonel Stewart would have been involved in that decision. Colonel Stewart was, in no way, in a position of authority vis-a-vis this special human rights -- the human rights rapporteur of the commission of the United Nations. I believe that that was a general matter of policy. But I must say that during my meetings with Colonel Blaskic, with Mr. Kordic, with Mr. Cerkez, that I did raise the fact, in general terms, that many of the witnesses could identify the perpetrators of these crimes and that the perpetrators of these crimes were in HVO uniforms and many of them were from local villages. So the matter was raised, although the specific 18 names may have not been mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just read you an excerpt from Colonel Stewart's diary of May the 4th, 1993. "Whilst hanging around the ECMM, I talked to Thomas Osorio and Payam Akhavan, both members of the U.N. Centre for Human Rights. They were investigating Ahmici. They told me that technically Tihomir Blaskic, Ante Valenta (vice-president HVO) and Pero Skopljak were at least guilty of complicity in genocide. In addition, Nenad Santic, Ivan Livancic, Kristo Zarko," and a word I can't read, "were part of the attacking HVO team." He then goes on to say: "I was incensed by this and agreed that we should raise the matter with Valenta and Blaskic without giving them names." Is that consistent with your recollection, sir?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do recall that we, on several occasions, discussed the fact that we should pressure the local leaders into undertaking a serious investigation with a view to punishing those responsible. I do not recall having come to an agreement with Colonel Stewart about mentioning names. The reason for that is that the names, the 18 names, were listed by Thomas Osorio on the same day that I was meeting with Colonel Blaskic, so we did not actually have those names available. It may be that on a subsequent occasion, Colonel Stewart may have decided that in his communications with these individuals in the HVO command, he would not bring up the names, but the names were simply not available at the time that I was meeting with Colonel Blaskic. The names were not available in the sense that we had already heard, from the witnesses in Zenica, that they could name specific individuals. One of them mentioned a school teacher, one of them mentioned Mr. so and so, but the names were not listed actually until the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you referred to a joint agreement or joint statement issued by Mate Boban, Alija Izetbegovic, and witnessed by Dr. Franjo Tudjman, dated April 25th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. That's previously been exhibited, Your Honours, as Exhibit D27/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you have knowledge of this joint statement before you conducted your tour through the Lasva Valley, sir?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we had knowledge of that statement, and indeed part of the reason the ECMM was encouraging us to go to the region is so that we could act as the independent, impartial commission envisaged in the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. So you were aware then, I take it, that as of April the 25th, 1993, the leading figure in the Croat community and the leading figure in the Muslim community had advocated the establishment of a joint commission to establish what had happened at Ahmici and other areas where atrocities had been committed; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct, in the same way that Radavan Karadzic and Vlatko Mladic regularly signed agreements explaining that they would comply with the Geneva Conventions. These agreements were a dime a dozen during the war, so we generally met them with considerable scepticism.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Nonetheless, you've described this development as commendable in your draft report?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course. The policy of the Special Rapporteur was always to encourage the parties to take their commitments seriously, but this was rarely the case, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Notwithstanding your foreknowledge of the recommendations from the political leaders of both sides actually even before you conducted your investigation, you decided not to disclose the names of the suspects to Colonel Blaskic or anyone else associated with the leadership of the Bosnian Croats in Central Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: As a field representative of the Special Rapporteur --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just "Yes" or "No," Mr. Akhavan.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would like to explain instead of giving a "Yes" or "No" answer, because I believe it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness explain.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not -- if you want a "Yes" or "No" answer, I did not, but the reason is I had no authority or mandate to do so. The information was transmitted to Geneva, where the Special Rapporteur made the decision to forward it to the commission of experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How would Colonel Blaskic be in a position to do an investigation of unnamed troops under his command when the percipient Muslim witnesses were beyond his ability to question, in your view?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, there was the possibility to still interview some of the Muslims which were still, at that date, being detained in various locations in the region under HVO control, and I think that clearly if there was a serious effort to investigate, the UNPROFOR soldiers could have easily escorted a representative of Colonel Blaskic or the HVO to interview the survivors in Zenica. In addition, there were still several survivors in the village of Ahmici and vicinity, members of the local Bosnian Croat population, including members of the HVO, who could also have been questioned. So there were, I think, many opportunities to investigate, and frankly speaking, I don't think it would take much imagination to figure out what had happened in Ahmici, based on the scale of the destruction and based on the fact that virtually every Muslim home was destroyed and none of the Croat homes were touched.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just to leave this point, you actually interviewed 100 to 150 survivors of Ahmici, did you not?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I personally did not interview them. My colleague, Thomas Osorio, did, and I accompanied him. I'm not sure if we interviewed each and every of the 100 to 150. We, I don't know, spent quite some time there, probably interviewed 30 or 40 people from different families at different times and locations to try and get a broad exposure to the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. But you never invited UNPROFOR yourself, I guess, to escort Colonel Blaskic and his team of investigators, whoever they might be, to interview these people that you had been given access to?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't think it was our business at all to get involved in such matters. We were there for one week to conduct an investigation. It was UNPROFOR that was present in the field. It was the HVO that assumed responsibility for the region. Our job, in general terms, was to alert them to the allegations, to the evidence which we had gathered, and to try to persuade them, with the very limited resources at our potential, to try and prevent the recurrence of such atrocities. How they chose to pursue such matters was, frankly speaking, beyond our control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, towards the end of the meeting that you had with Colonel Blaskic, and I'm finished with him now, I believe that you gave some testimony that a man named Anto or Ante Valenta came into the meeting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that was his name. He was introduced to us as, I believe, vice-president. I have this in my notes here. Yes, Anto Valenta, vice-president HVO from Travnik, and he was in Vitez because of the dangerous situation in Travnik. I believe the dangerous situation referred to the Serbs, because Colonel Blaskic had also explained that he had moved his headquarters from Travnik to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Once again, Mr. Akhavan, I hate to interrupt you, but really it's very simple. When a question is asked like that, "Did you meet Anto Valenta" --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- the answer is either "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you made notes of that meeting, and those appear on pages 32 and 33 --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- your notes which we've marked as Exhibit 65/1, I believe. All right. You would concede, would you not, that there's absolutely no reference there to the sorts of propagandising and extreme views to which you testified a few days ago?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would not bother to take notes which would have no factual relevance to our report, but it did clearly leave an impression on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In your statement of 1995, you told the investigators from the Prosecution, for whom you actually worked, that you pretty much ignored Mr. Valenta; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. After I heard what he had to say, I decided that there wasn't really anything to be gained from entering into a discussion with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Therefore, you proceeded to make two pages of notes about what he did say.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure if those notes are about what he has said. I simply have taken a note there indicating Anto Valenta, who he was. Whenever someone entered the meeting that I felt was sufficiently important, I would try to note down who that person was. But then I believe from the point where I say "Commander of Vitez Brigade," I'm not sure if that refers to what Anto Valenta told me or whether I'm now returning back to what Colonel Blaskic was telling me. I don't suppose he was commander of the Vitez Brigade, so this is probably a continuation of what Colonel Blaskic was telling me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There is no reference --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is actually the meeting with Mario Cerkez. Anto Valenta probably would have come towards the end of my discussion with Colonel Blaskic, so I noted his presence, simply that he had moved to Vitez because of the dangerous situation in Travnik, and then you see at the left margin "Mario Cerkez," which has probably been written down for me either by himself or someone who was present at the meeting, just to get the correct spelling, and then begins the interview with him, which was actually at a separate time and location from that of Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let's turn, if I may, then to your interview with Mr. Cerkez. I will leave most of the questions on this topic to my colleague, Mr. Kovacic, but I do have a few questions for you in this regard. Did you use the same sort of cross-examination technique on Mr. Cerkez that you had used on Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not use cross-examination techniques such as those being used against me. I think I conducted an interview, and where the answers were evasive, on occasion, I would try to, if you like, focus the discussion so as not to waste any of our times, because, indeed, the time was very limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did Captain Dundas-Whatley ever tell you that he was completely embarrassed by your cross-examination technique in connection with Mr. Cerkez that day?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not engage in a cross-examination technique, but I knew that Dundas-Whatley was not pleased by the spirit of the meetings, because their mandate and interest was very different than mine. The British Battalion was trying to create some sort of trust --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did he ever tell you that he was embarrassed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him finish, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Dundas-Whatley, understandably, and the UNPROFOR in general, their mandate was not respect for human rights; their mandate was military security. In order to achieve their objective, they had to have a relationship of trust and confidence with the local HVO commanders. In our case, our job was to put forward embarrassing and difficult issues, such as the fact that the HVO may have slaughtered several hundred civilians. This was never, even under the best of circumstances, going to create a good air between the human rights representative and the person in question. I believe that the meeting with Cerkez was not in cross-examination style, but it was also not a pleasant meeting. None of the meetings that I had were pleasant meetings, if that's what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No. Here's what I'm asking: In the statement that Captain Matthew Dundas-Whatley gave to the Prosecution on February the 19th, 1995, here's what he had to say. He was taken to see Cerkez. "DW stated that during a 45-minute interview, he became embarrassed as PA," that's you, "cross-examined Cerkez."

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I recall that statement of Dundas-Whatley. I'm not sure if Mr. Whatley is a lawyer, so I would take his use of the word "cross-examination" with a grain of salt, but it was clear that there was not a good spirit at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This was the first time that you had met Mr. Cerkez, I take it?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You told him that he was responsible to conduct a full investigation regarding the activities of the soldiers under his command; right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: During your interview with Mr. Cerkez, he never once mentioned to you the name Dario Kordic, did he?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe the name of Dario Kordic came up during the meeting. As I said, I had reviewed the question of authority in the region in every occasion, but I don't recall specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. Your notes don't reflect any mention of the name Dario Kordic by Mr. Cerkez during your interview of him, do they?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, they don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That brings us to the 15-minute meeting that you had with Dario Kordic on May the 5th.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You met Mr. Kordic once, did you not?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the meeting degenerated into a shouting match, with each one of you jabbing fingers at one another?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't believe that there was shouting. There may have been finger-pointing, largely on his part. I was basically escorted by one member of the British Battalion into the meeting. There were several soldiers, both in the antechamber and in his room, carrying guns and rifles, and I would say, if anything, he was in the position to be pointing fingers at me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you use the same interrogation style as you had used with Mr. Cerkez shortly before?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think the witness has accepted that he used an interrogation style. So if you will rephrase that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Here's what Captain Dundas-Whatley has to say about the meeting: "After calling at the local police HQ, DK," Mr. Kordic, "appeared, but on this occasion, when PA started his interrogation-style interview, this resulted in DK going into some long statements and pointing his fingers aggressively at PA." Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would agree that, as I said earlier, he was the one pointing fingers at me. I was not necessarily pointing them back. I would also agree that the interview was very vigorous, if you want to call that interrogation, but if you look at my notes, you will see that most of the interview, which changed towards the end, was Dario Kordic telling me about the HDZ --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Excuse me? I'm sorry, sir. It is the fourth last page --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Page 34, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: -- which says "Dario Kordic, 5 May" at the top. Dundas-Whatley was extremely afraid, for some reason or other, of Dario Kordic. He was extremely deferential, and obviously, it was very difficult to get an audience with Dario Kordic, which is why we had to wait some one hour outside of his office to get the meeting with him. As I said, he was extremely deferential and respectful. The first part of the meeting with Dario Kordic, as reflected by the notes, indicates that we discussed relatively, how do you say, issues which were not controversial. He was explaining to me what the HDZ is, what his relationship is with the HVO, and his overall view about the politics of the region and the status of Herceg-Bosna, in what I considered to be a very sophisticated presentation, and it was only towards the end that I brought up the issue of Ahmici and the atrocities, and his response was such that it was clear that the meeting was going to be a waste of time, which is why it was terminated somewhat prematurely, largely on his part, not on my part, because he was the one who decided when it begins and when it ends.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that he threw you out of his office?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that he threw you out of his office?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't think he physically threw me out, but I think that he expressed his irritation sufficiently that I realised that I'm no longer welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He told you that, in his opinion, HVO soldiers could not have been involved in the events at Ahmici, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. To use his exact words, he said: "Our soldiers are good Christians who would never commit such acts."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Kordic wearing a crucifix that day, as was his custom?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall. I know he was wearing a military uniform, but I don't remember the cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When you say "a military uniform," sir, do you mean just regular fatigues?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Camouflage pants and top.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did he have any rank insignia that you could see?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is it my understanding that it was during the course of this unpleasant, confrontational, 15-minute exchange that this Croat politician told you that maybe the events of Ahmici were the work of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: At first, he suggested they were Serbs, and then he suggested they were the Muslims themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You didn't make notes of that, did you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, because I found not only his explanation but also the demeanour on his face so mocking and unreasonable that I didn't even bother. And anyway, it was a standard explanation which I had been given also by Colonel Blaskic. To me, the point was what is the response of the Bosnian Croat authorities in the region to these allegations, and all I needed to do for the purposes of a report was to state what their explanations were and whether, in our opinion, they were reasonable or credible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you personally angry and irritated that Mr. Kordic didn't treat you seriously?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Personally, I'm not sure if it was personal. I think that I was clearly moved by what I'd seen in Ahmici and environs, and I found his arrogance and contempt disturbing, if that's the case, in addition to some of the explanations that he was giving.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The explanation that you were given, I think you previously testified about this, but specifically the explanation that Mr. Kordic gave you was a relatively standard explanation, as you actually put in your report of May the 19th, 1993, Exhibit Z942, paragraph 12. On page 4, it says: "Leading Croat political figures in the Lasva Valley region are reported as constantly using the media as a means of demonising other ethnic groups. Atrocities against Muslims or Serbs are rarely, if ever, reported and are usually blamed on Serb forces or an unknown group of extremists."

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Which paragraph is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Paragraph 12. It's one of your draft reports, not your actual final report that was introduced as --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I don't have that here. Yes, that is probably reflecting the explanations which they had given us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, is it accepted that Mr. Kordic gave that explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It is not, no. The explanation that Mr. Kordic came up with was he did not mention that Serbs were responsible for the incidents in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did he suggest that it may have been the Muslims themselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that that is contested as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, you've heard that suggested, that Mr. Kordic did not give either explanation.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did he do so?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I distinctly remember, Your Honour, that when he consistently said that the HVO was not capable of these atrocities or had not committed them, then I pushed him to explain to me who, indeed, had, at which point he suggested that possibly the Serbs may have done it under the cover of night or that the Muslims themselves may have done it to win some sort of sympathy. I don't believe that he categorically asserted that either the Serbs or Muslims have done it, but he offered them as two possible explanations, based on the assumption that the HVO could not possibly have committed the crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, how long did the basic introductions take, Mr. Akhavan, during this 15-minute interview that you had with Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I suppose possibly half of the meeting. And I'm not sure if the meeting was exactly 15 minutes, but it was a short meeting, especially when we went beyond the discussion of the HDZ and HVO and some of the issues which Mr. Kordic enjoyed discussing about and we got into the discussion of responsibility for the atrocities in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In your June 1995 statement, you said, quote, and this is on page 4: "The entire meeting may have lasted about 15 minutes." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Page --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Page 4.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry, page 4 of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your June the 23rd, 1995 --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was a short meeting. I don't remember exactly how long, but it was probably in that range.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So about seven and a half minutes were spent on the basic introductions?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who was your interpreter?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who was present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: The interpreter, I believe Dundas-Whatley, and I believe that there were also some soldiers, HVO soldiers, which may have been present. I'm not sure if they left the room. I believe they stayed in the room during the meeting, three or four of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Could you just describe how the remaining seven and a half minutes of the interview proceeded after the introductions had been made?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I think it was very straightforward. I explained that my colleague and I, over the past several days, had overwhelming evidence that the HVO had been involved in killing large numbers of civilians in Ahmici, in Vitez, in neighbouring villages, that there was extensive destruction of property and so on and so forth, some of which we had actually witnessed ourselves, and that I was interested in knowing what he had to say about this evidence, if he intended to do anything about it. And I explained that the purpose of the meeting was to offer him, as the most senior official of Herceg-Bosna in the region, to give us his side of the story, following which he began explaining how the HVO soldiers could not possibly have done it because of their exceptional moral standards and so on and so forth, after which I repeated that all the evidence indicated that HVO soldiers were responsible, after which he gave the explanation that possibly the Serbs or the Mujahedin or Muslims or others may have done it themselves, after which I suggested to him that that was not a satisfactory explanation. He, I recall, smiled and said, "Well, I will try to persuade you with another explanation," and at that point I basically said, "Mr. Kordic, this is a waste of time. This is not a credible explanation." And I explained to him that he, as the most senior figure in the region, must see to it that these matters are fully investigated, with a view to preventing them in the future, and that if we were not to be given any alternate explanation or anything that would persuade us otherwise, we would write in our report that the HVO forces were indeed responsible and we would wait and see whether the local authorities would take any action for the purpose of making our assessment of who is responsible. Not who is responsible in an individual sense but who is responsible in a global sense, which party to the conflict is responsible. At that point, the shouting and finger-pointing on his part began, and I think I did a reasonably good job of controlling my response, in part because I had the feeling that I may even be taken out and shot right there and then. So we ended the meeting rather quickly. I don't think that I ever said anything to him that was directly insulting or raised my voice in a way that could be considered as shouting. I think it was largely on his part. I believe that was the end of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So within the first 15 minutes of your meeting this leading political figure, you instructed him that in your view, you did not find his explanations credible?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In 15 minutes of first meeting the man, you called him a liar, basically, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: "Liar" could be one word, but I think I simply told him, for his sake, that if he wanted a fair hearing, if he wanted a report which at least gave their side of the story, that he should try to give me a better explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That might be an appropriate place to break, Your Honour. I might say that we've made better progress than I had anticipated today, so I would think that on Thursday, I would not be more than 45 minutes with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last witness, nothing to do with Mr. Akhavan's evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Akhavan, would you be back, please, when you're informed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you would like to go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm informed that the last witness has been able to look at either originals or copies of some of Dooley's diaries to suggest that the date of the stopping of the convoy was the 28th of April. I'm not intending to keep him here longer tomorrow to deal with that. We know that the date can be further verified by consideration of either The Sunday Times or whatever it is for the following Sunday. So it may be if that date is not contentious --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The date is not contentious, Your Honour, may it please, but I would like to know if we found the newspaper article that he made reference to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, we certainly haven't found the newspaper article yet, but I imagine that can be done by us or, more probably, by others with easier access to the internet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Tomorrow morning. Half past nine, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 1.02 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 4th day of August, 1999, at 9.30 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
